subject: chemistry

moments.title: Moseley's law
moments.body: Moseley, 26, shows X-ray frequencies from elements scale with nuclear charge — atomic number, not atomic weight. He reorders Co-Ni and Te-I in the periodic table and shows there are exactly 4 gaps (elements 43, 61, 72, 75) still to find.
moments.takeaway: Atomic number, not atomic weight, organises the periodic table.

moments.title: Moseley dies at Gallipoli
moments.body: Moseley enlists despite Rutherford's pleas; he is killed by a sniper at Gallipoli at age 27. Asimov later writes: 'In view of what he might still have accomplished, his death might well have been the most costly single death of the War to mankind generally.'
moments.takeaway: One of the most promising scientists of his generation, killed at 27.

moments.title: Britain's Pittsburgh policy
moments.body: After Moseley's death, the UK introduces a policy of never assigning prominent scientists to combat roles. The policy holds in WWII.
moments.takeaway: A single death changes military policy.

moments.title: The four missing elements
moments.body: Technetium (43, 1937), promethium (61, 1945), hafnium (72, 1923), rhenium (75, 1925) are all eventually found — exactly the gaps Moseley predicted.
moments.takeaway: Moseley's table is verified, element by element.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The periodic table is now ordered by atomic number. Synchrotron X-ray sources continue Moseley's tradition. He is generally considered to have lost a clear Nobel due to his death.
now.open_questions: Will element 119 (ununennium) ever be confirmed? How is the periodic table best extended?

reflection: Moseley's death at 27 cost the world incalculable science. How should states protect scientists during war?
